chapter_theme: Songs at Siruvai (சிறுவை, சிறுவாபுரி): a plea that Murugan come dancing with his peacock in sight of all the gods, a litany of salutations, a plea to escape birth through the feet that opened the way of silence, and a confession about courtesans with a long string of the goddess's names; the town is praised as the place where two boys fought Rama.

724.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come dancing with his peacock so that Indra is resettled in his city, the demons are changed, the gods rejoice, Siva who dances with the goddess, Ganesha and Uma are glad, and the world, the sages, all in the eight directions, Brahma and Vishnu with Lakshmi see him before them. The praise names the lotus-eyed bridegroom of the gods' daughter, full of wisdom, whose vel split the sea and the mountain, with a pearl-hung chest, dear to cool Tamil, at Siruvai where he dwells in his devotees' hearts.
724.nuance: The plea asks for nothing for the poet: it asks for an epiphany, Murugan coming in sight of everyone (எதிர்காண). தண்டமிழின் மிகுநேய, the lover of cool Tamil, and அடியார்கள் சிந்தையது குடியான, who lives in his devotees' minds, frame the shrine.

725.reading: A litany of salutations (நமோ நம) to Murugan: to the cool lotus feet, to the one who delights in Narada's songs, to the lover of the cock and peacock, the crest the Vedas seek, the essence of the Agamas, the commander of the gods' army, the axe that cuts sins so that souls reach their goal, the terror of the asura king, the child of Parvati, ending in a plea for grace. The praise names the brother of the elephant-faced one, the one dear to Siva, the nephew of Lakshmi's lord, the six faces like full moons, praised by Vishnu and Brahma, and Siruvapuri, richer than the gods' city and Alaka.
725.nuance: The whole first half is salutation, not plea, until the closing அருள்தாராய். பாதக நீவு குடாரா, the axe that cuts away sin so the soul reaches its goal (கதி தோய), is the one line about the poet's need.

726.reading: The poet asks that he not perish trusting in birth, which has no hold: coming down into the inert body, crowding into pathless places, wandering in sickness and sorrow, grieving under growing evil deeds and roaming through every state; that the lotus feet which opened the rare way of silence never leave his mind; and whether, desiring the sweet service that men and gods offer, he will be counted Murugan's servant. The praise seems to tell how Murugan, mindful of a demon in a cave who troubled the sages, came in an instant on the peacock and, delighted, accepted Tamil, and names Siruvai, rich as Alaka, the town where two boys fought Rama with his elephants and foot soldiers and won.
726.nuance: மோன வழி திறந்த நளின பாதம்: the feet themselves open the way of silence. The cave (பிலன்), the demon, the sudden coming on the peacock and the Tamil (தமிழ் புனைந்த) may point to Nakkirar freed from a demon's cave by his Murugan poem, but the text does not name him. The boys who fought Rama are the shrine's own legend, presumably Lava and Kusa.

727.reading: The poet speaks of women with spear eyes who sell love for money, who abuse a man without regard for the hour and are called whores, and of himself, a small man wandering in desire for them, and asks that he never forget the feet worshipped by Vishnu, Brahma, Siva, the gods, the sages and Indra, that he worship desiring the good path to Siva's bliss, and that his troubles be removed. The praise names Murugan as the child given by the goddess under a string of names (Nila Sundari, Komali, Yamali, Narani who dances, Purani, Sulini, Malini, Uma, Kali, Sivakama Sundari), the teacher by Siva's grace, nephew of Vishnu who lies on the banyan leaf to keep the world steady, at Siruvapuri with its golden towers.
727.nuance: வேசி என்பவர், காதலின் பொருள் மேவின பாதகர்: here the women are named outright as harlots who trade love for money. The praise is mostly a list of the goddess's names, so it centres on Shakti more than on Murugan. சிவபோக நல் நூல் நெறி, the good path to Siva's bliss, is set against the women's போகம்.
